query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled surface mechanical treatment that induces dynamic amorphization and refines the near‐surface microstructure into an ultra‐nanocrystalline layer will enable the CoCrFeNi alloy to maintain low friction and wear rates from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with a comparatively coarse-grained, untreated near-surface structure that degrades under high-temperature sliding.
generation.intervention: Apply a single-step surface mechanical treatment (e.g., a severe plastic deformation process) designed to cause dynamic amorphization and nano-crystallization at the alloy's surface.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted over a temperature range of room temperature to 800 °C, under varying loads and in an oxidizing (air) environment.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline, partially amorphized layer at the near-surface region.
generation.mechanism: The refined layer decreases shear strength and enhances resistance to thermal degradation by maintaining a stable microstructure, thereby reducing friction and wear. This nano-structured surface is expected to offer continuous self-lubricating properties across the wide temperature range by preventing the coarser grain growth and oxidation seen in untreated alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: The mechanically treated CoCrFeNi samples will exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rates compared to untreated samples across the full temperature range, with the beneficial ultra-nanocrystalline layer remaining intact even at high temperatures.
generation.baseline: Untreated CoCrFeNi alloys, which show increased friction and wear at elevated temperatures due to coarser grains and oxidation-related degradation.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is anticipated under sliding conditions and loads similar to previous tribological tests; the performance in highly aggressive oxidizing environments or under extreme mechanical loads remains to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal treatment parameters to reliably form and preserve the ultra-nanocrystalline layer at 800 °C are not yet defined, and the long-term stability of this layer under cyclic loading and thermal fluctuations is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of CoCrFeNi alloy samples: one group will receive the surface mechanical treatment and the other will remain untreated as a control. Subject both groups to identical sliding wear tests across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under controlled load and environmental conditions.
measurements: Coefficient of friction throughout the temperature range
Post-test microstructural analysis (using STEM/SEM to detect grain size refinement and amorphization of the near-surface region)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not consistently show significantly lower friction coefficients and wear rates across the full temperature range compared to the untreated controls, or if microstructural analysis fails to confirm the presence of an ultra-nanocrystalline, amorphized surface layer, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
